proof_nl:
Fix an integer n>1, a real number x, and an integer z. We prove that f_n(x+z)=f_n(x).

Recall the standard floor identity: for every real t and every integer m, floor(t+m)=floor(t)+m. Indeed, if floor(t)=a, then a<=t<a+1, so a+m<=t+m<a+m+1, hence floor(t+m)=a+m.

Now for each k in {1,2,...,n}, since kz is an integer, we have
floor(k(x+z))=floor(kx+kz)=floor(kx)+kz.
Also, for k=n,
floor(n(x+z))=floor(nx+nz)=floor(nx)+nz.
Therefore
f_n(x+z)=floor(n(x+z)) - sum_{k=1}^n floor(k(x+z))/k
= floor(nx)+nz - sum_{k=1}^n (floor(kx)+kz)/k
= floor(nx)+nz - sum_{k=1}^n floor(kx)/k - sum_{k=1}^n z
= floor(nx)+nz - sum_{k=1}^n floor(kx)/k - nz
= floor(nx) - sum_{k=1}^n floor(kx)/k
= f_n(x).
So f_n is invariant under integer shifts: f_n(x+z)=f_n(x) for all real x and all integers z.
solver_summary: Apply floor(t+m)=floor(t)+m with m=kz and m=nz termwise in the definition of f_n; the nz contributions cancel, giving f_n(x+z)=f_n(x).
vetter_reason: The proof correctly establishes integer-shift invariance of f_n by applying floor(t+m)=floor(t)+m to each term, then cancelling the added nz contribution against the sum of z over k=1..n. The argument is complete and matches the lemma and semantic sketch exactly.
